title: Interfaces and Singularity: one building, any interface
description: A theory by George Billam: a building should exist once, as a single open source written in code. Revit, SketchUp, Rhino, Grasshopper, a chat window and an AI agent all read and write the same source, and none of them owns it.
content: Interfaces and Singularity is a theory by George Billam (first set out 30/10/2026). A building should exist once, as a single open source written in code: the singularity. Every piece of software becomes just an interface on it. Revit, SketchUp, Rhino, Grasshopper, a chat window, a site tablet and an AI agent all read and write the same source, and none of them owns it.
One source holds the building. Anything can write to it, anything can ask it questions. The software is the interface, not the owner.

The web shows how this works. A website is HTML; Chrome and Safari show it differently, and no website belongs to Chrome. Buildings have never had that split, because the authoring software and the data have always been sold as one thing.
It pairs with the companion theory, Ask-Built: Ask-Built is the way out (a drawing is a query on the model), Interfaces and Singularity is the way in (modelling is editing one shared source).
The building block

Generative building design will not come from driving Revit through MCP. That route makes an AI operate software built for a human with a mouse: it clicks through dialogs, waits on regeneration, and stalls when a warning pops up. The AI is boxed into the platform's way of thinking.

The singularity is made of a more sympathetic building block: a component written as code. A wall, a door, a stair core or a whole shop unit is a small, readable definition holding three things: geometry, or the rules that produce it; data (product, fire rating, acoustic rating, cost, supplier, maintenance); and intent and constraints (why it is the way it is, so a change that breaks the reason is caught).

Because it is text, an agent can iterate it the way it iterates software: propose a change, run the checks, keep what passes, try again. Hundreds of options can be generated, tested against the brief, Approved Documents B and M and the landlord's rules, and ranked before a human looks at one. Only then does it need an interface, and it can be shown in Revit, or any other interface, as a native-looking object.
Agents inside the model

Once the building is a single open source rather than a locked file, agents can live inside it rather than poking at it from outside. They run continuously, floor by floor, element by element, the way a site manager walks a job, except every walk is complete and takes seconds.

A fire agent checks compartment lines, travel distances, door ratings and penetrations. An access agent checks clear widths, turning circles, level thresholds and Part M routes. A coordination agent finds clashes and proposes fixes rather than just flagging them. A cost agent tracks live quantities against budget as the design moves. A compliance agent logs every change against the brief, landlord rules and Approved Documents for the golden thread.

The agents don't wait to be asked. A change made by anyone, in any interface, triggers the relevant agents, and the result is waiting for review: accepted, rejected, or sent back with a reason. The designer's job shifts from producing and checking to deciding.
The interface is a skin

AutoCAD users used to switch between the ribbon and the classic menus. Same drawing, same commands, different face. Interfaces and Singularity says the whole modelling application becomes that kind of choice.

AI is making software cheap to rebuild. An interface that looks and behaves like Revit, SketchUp, Rhino or Grasshopper can be produced over an open building source, so each person works in the face they think best in: the technologist detailing in a Revit-style interface; the designer massing in SketchUp or Rhino; the computational designer in a Grasshopper-style graph; the client or subcontractor in plain conversation or a tick-box form; the agents in the raw code.

All of them edit the same building at the same time. Training stops being "learn Revit" and becomes "learn the building". A practice no longer has to pick a platform and live with it; a new starter brings whichever interface they already know.
What would have to be true

One geometry engine everyone trusts. If five interfaces edit the same wall, they must agree where the opening cuts it. Either the source stores the resolved geometry, or there is one open engine every interface calls. This is the main reason vendors keep ownership today.
Intent travels, not just shape. IFC carries the finished geometry; a door exported from Revit cannot flex like a Revit door. The building block has to carry its rules.
Every edit is signed. Anyone or anything can write, so every change needs an author, a time, a reason and a check. Git for buildings. This is also what the golden thread asks for.

Someone forces it open. Vendors earn from owning the format. Openness most likely arrives through regulation, a large client or government mandate, or open-source tools becoming good enough to win anyway.
Interfaces are built, not copied. "Feels like Revit" is fine; copying Revit's code or look wholesale runs into licence terms and intellectual property.
What already exists

IFC5 (buildingSMART) is a JSON-based rework of IFC aiming at shared ownership through layers and incremental updates, but it is still alpha and built for exchange rather than as the live source you design in. Speckle offers open, versioned object data with connectors into Revit, Rhino, AutoCAD and others, but authoring stays in each app and data is translated in and out. Autodesk's AEC Data Model breaks Revit and DWG files into cloud-queryable object data, but it is open on Autodesk's terms, in Autodesk's cloud. None of these makes the open source the master building with every application as an interface on it.
Soundbites
"The building is the source code. Revit is just one interface."
"We're going to switch between Revit and Rhino the way we used to switch between the ribbon and classic menus."
"Generative design won't come from an AI driving Revit. It'll come from a building block an AI can rewrite."
"Stop learning software. Learn the building."
"Agents don't check the model at the end. They live in it."

title: Ask-Built: a drawing is an answer, not a deliverable
description: A theory by George Billam: if the information model is complete and trusted, the drawing stops being a deliverable and becomes an answer. Nobody produces a drawing until someone on the job asks a question that needs one.
content: Ask-Built is a theory by George Billam (first set out 30/10/2026): if the information model is complete and trusted, the drawing stops being a deliverable and becomes an answer. Nobody produces a drawing until someone on the job asks a question that needs one. Then it is generated for that person, that package and that moment, and thrown away when the question changes.
The name is a play on "as-built". As-built records what was built after the fact. Ask-Built says the documentation of a building should be produced by asking, not by issuing.
The one-line version: a drawing is an answer to a question someone hasn't asked yet, so stop answering in advance.
The theory

Today we push drawings: a design team decides in advance which plans, sections, elevations and details every trade might need, draws them all, revises them all, and issues them in packages. Most of that effort answers questions nobody asks, and every change has to be chased through every sheet that shows it. Ask-Built flips this from push to pull.

Where a building information model holds the design to the level the job needs, the model is the deliverable and every drawing is a query on it. Drawings are generated on demand, scoped to the person asking, and carry the model revision they were drawn from.

Where it came from: the question started in conversation about AI agents driving Revit through MCP. If an agent can already open a model and produce sheets on instruction, the next step is obvious: why instruct it at all? A subcontractor says "my package is the data containment, show me what I need to install it" and gets exactly that, drawn from the live model.

Five principles: the model is the only source of truth (drawings are views, never records); no question, no drawing (nothing is drawn speculatively); scoped to the asker (the containment installer sees containment and nothing else); disposable and stamped (every generated drawing carries its model revision and expires when the model moves on); the asking is the audit trail (who asked what, when, and what they were shown is itself a record, closer to the Building Safety Act's golden thread than a register of issued PDFs).
How it works on a job

Take a fit-out where the data containment installer starts on Monday. Today they get the full electrical set and find their scope. Under Ask-Built they ask for their package and get one drawing: containment routes, setting-out, fixings and the interfaces with ceilings and other services, nothing else. A model change retires the drawing instead of triggering a reissue.
What already exists

The "no drawings" half of this is not new: Scandinavia has built bridges, hydropower stations and city-scale schemes with the model as the contract document, including a 634-metre bridge built with no drawings at all (Randselva Bridge, Norway) and the Slussen redevelopment in Stockholm. What those projects did not solve is the person on site who cannot or will not navigate a model. Ask-Built's contribution is the second half: keep the drawing, but make it a generated answer to a trade's question rather than a pre-issued sheet.

Total BIM (Chalmers University) makes the model the legally binding construction document but asks site workers to use model-viewer software, keeping a structural engineer on site to pull measurements. Ask-Built moves that job to the system. Drawingless / Zero Drawings (Sweco) removes the drawing entirely; Ask-Built keeps it as the trade's preferred interface and removes only the pre-production of it. Level of Information Need (BS EN ISO 7817-1) is the closest cousin in UK standards: it defines what information each party needs; Ask-Built is the delivery mechanism.
Objections

"Subbies aren't technical enough to query a model." Ask-Built asks less of them than today. They currently find their scope across a full drawing set and a spec. Under Ask-Built they tick what their package includes, or say it in plain words, and get one drawing.

"Drawings are the contract documents." True for nearly every UK project today. Ask-Built needs the model, plus the rules for generating views, to be the contract document. Until then it runs as a production method sitting behind conventional issued sets.
"AI will hallucinate a dimension." Ask-Built does not let AI invent geometry. The AI chooses which elements, views and annotations answer the question; dimensions and positions come from the model.

"Who carries liability for a drawing nobody drew?" The designer is liable for the model and for the view rules; the system records exactly what was shown to whom. That is a cleaner position than today, where a superseded sheet on site is a common cause of error.

"Models are never complete enough." Correct, and the theory says so. Ask-Built raises the stakes on model quality. Where the model is thin, the system should refuse the question and flag the gap, not guess.
Using it in talks

The 60-second version: "We spend a huge share of fee producing drawings in case someone needs them. I call the alternative Ask-Built. If the model is good enough, a drawing is just an answer to a question. So don't answer in advance. Let the containment installer say 'show me my package' and generate exactly that, from the live model, stamped with the revision. The Scandinavians have already proved you can build a 634-metre bridge with no drawings at all. What they hadn't cracked is the operative who doesn't want to drive a 3D viewer. AI cracks that. The drawing survives; it just stops being something we produce and starts being something the job asks for."

Soundbites: "A drawing is an answer, not a deliverable." "As-built tells you what happened. Ask-Built tells you what you need." "We don't print a website for every visitor. Why do we print a building for every trade?" "Stop answering questions nobody has asked." "The skill barrier should sit with the system, not the operative."
Companion theory: Ask-Built covers the way out of the model. The way in, one open building source with every application as an interface on it, is set out in Interfaces and Singularity.
